Stage 1: flash, bring up and tune

Flash the PID firmware, check the IMU and the motor direction, tune the gains over serial, and test it against the pass criteria.

Read this first: designed and simulated, not builtDesigned and simulated. Not printed, not built. The firmware compiles for the ESP32 but has not run on hardware. Every motor and mass figure is an estimate carried over from the published Tailwhip. Like the rest of Tailwhip, the design, its code and these pages were generated with AI. Measure what the pages tell you to, check each step with a meter, expect to fix things, and build at your own risk, especially around the 18650 cells.

The sketch

stage1_balance.ino on GitHub Download the sketch

The firmware

firmware/stage1_balance/stage1_balance.ino, board "ESP32 Dev Module". No radio, no laptop in the loop.

  • 400 Hz loop: read the IMU, complementary filter for pitch, PID, one PWM pair to the MX1508.
  • Arms itself when held within 5 degrees of upright for half a second; lets go past 22 degrees.
  • Serial at 115200: gains, trim, direction flip, save to flash, a 50 Hz CSV stream, an open-loop motor test.
  • Default gains come from sim.py tune: kp 1.62, kd 0.37, kv 1.94, kx 0.11 (per rad, rad/s, m/s, m).
  • The filter and PID are the same code path sim.py simulates. Change one, change the other.

Flash it

Use the same toolchain as the full robot (its setup): the Arduino IDE or arduino-cli with the esp32 core, board ESP32 Dev Module. The sketch needs no extra libraries. It has been checked to compile with arduino-cli and esp32 core 3.3.12. From the top of the repository:

arduino-cli compile -b esp32:esp32:esp32 stage1/firmware/stage1_balance
arduino-cli upload  -b esp32:esp32:esp32 -p /dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX stage1/firmware/stage1_balance
arduino-cli monitor -p /dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX -c baudrate=115200

Type help in the serial monitor for the commands:

kp|kd|ki|kv|kx|dz <value>   gains and dead-zone compensation
trim <deg>                  balance point (+ if it creeps forward)
dir <1|-1>                  flip if the wheels drive the wrong way
show | save | defaults      print, store in flash, restore
stream <0|1>                CSV at 50 Hz: ms,pitch_deg,rate_dps,u,v_est,vbat
motor <u> <ms>              bench: run the motor at u (-1..1) for ms, robot off the ground
cal                         recalibrate the gyro (hold it still)

Bring-up

Do the power-up checklist on the Circuit and wiring page first: it flashes this sketch at step 0 and checks the IMU and the motor one connection at a time. Then:

  1. Set the Mini360 to 5.0 V on the bench before it touches the ESP32.
  2. Flash, open the serial monitor, type show. Tilt it forward: pitch must go positive.
  3. Wheels off the ground, motor 0.3 1000. The wheels must turn the way that would drive it forward; if not, dir -1. Count turns in a motor 1 3000 run to get the no-load speed.
  4. Hold it upright and still through power-on (gyro calibration), then let it arm in your hands.
  5. Tune: creeps one way, change trim; falls over slowly, raise kp; shakes hard, lower kd; runs away, raise kv. save when it stands.
  6. stream 1, log 20 s, and compare the wobble with out/plot_nominal.png.

Pass criteria

Stage 1 passes when the real robot stands for 60 s on a flat floor, recovers when released from 8 degrees, and survives light pokes; and its measured wobble, motor speed and dead zone have been fed back into sim.py.

After stage 1

Stage 2 adds a second TT motor, wheel sensors and a bar that holds the body at a lean (see the three stages); it is planned but not designed yet. Stage 1's core, electronics and firmware carry into it. Until then, the next step is the full robot: start at the Build plan.
